lessons.title: The First Program
intro: In 1972, Dennis Ritchie at Bell Labs created C to write the Unix operating system. It ran on a PDP-11, a computer the size of a fridge, and people used it through terminals like this one.
In 1978, Brian Kernighan and Ritchie wrote the book "The C Programming Language". Its first example printed two words: hello, world. Programmers have started every new language with it ever since.
Every C program starts in a function called main. Everything between its curly braces { } runs from top to bottom. printf prints text, and \n starts a new line.

exercises.explanation: Ritchie built C around 1972 to rewrite Unix, together with Ken Thompson.

exercises.prompt: Where does a C program start running?
options: On the first line of the file
exercises.explanation: The computer looks for main and runs what's inside its braces.

exercises.prompt: What does \n do inside the text?
exercises.explanation: \n is the newline character. Without it, the next output would continue on the same line.

exercises.prompt: What do the curly braces { } do?
options: They hold the statements that belong to main
exercises.explanation: Braces group statements into a block, here the body of main.

exercises.prompt: Put the lines in order for a program that prints hi.
exercises.explanation: First the #include, then main with its opening brace, the statements, and the closing brace last.

exercises.prompt: What was the first program in Kernighan and Ritchie's book?
exercises.explanation: It's been the first program in nearly every programming book since.

lessons.title: Statements and Semicolons
intro: Every statement in C ends with a semicolon ;. It tells the compiler: this instruction is complete. Forget one, and the compiler stops with an error, usually pointing at the line.
#include <stdio.h> at the top loads the standard input/output library, where printf lives. return 0; at the end tells Unix the program finished without problems.
Text in double quotes is a string. Each printf can print a little or a lot, and nothing moves to a new line unless you write \n.

exercises.prompt: What ends every statement in C?
exercises.explanation: The semicolon marks the end. A new line alone isn't enough.
Neither printf has a \n, so both letters land on the same line.

exercises.prompt: This program doesn't compile. Which line is wrong?
exercises.explanation: The printf is missing its semicolon at the end.

options: It loads the library with printf
exercises.explanation: stdio.h describes the standard input and output functions, like printf and scanf.
Every statement ends with a semicolon.

exercises.prompt: What does return 0; at the end of main mean?
exercises.explanation: Unix programs report 0 for success. Other numbers mean something went wrong.

lessons.title: Compile and Run
intro: C isn't run line by line like BASIC. First the compiler translates the whole program into machine code. On Unix, you type cc hello.c, and if there are no errors, you get a program called a.out.
Then you run it by typing ./a.out. Compiling catches many mistakes before the program even starts, and the machine code runs very fast.
Comments start with /* and end with */. The compiler skips them; they're notes for people. (Modern C also allows // until the end of the line.)

exercises.prompt: What does cc hello.c do on Unix?
options: Compiles the program into machine code
exercises.explanation: cc is the C compiler. It creates a.out, the program you can run.

exercises.prompt: Which file does cc create if you don't name one?
exercises.explanation: a.out stands for "assembler output", a name from the early Unix days.

options: Many mistakes are found before the program runs, and the result is fast machine code
exercises.explanation: The compiler checks the whole program first. That's why C programs ran fast even on slow computers.
The middle line is inside a comment, so it never runs.

exercises.prompt: Turn this line into a comment.
exercises.explanation: Comments start with /* and end with */.

exercises.prompt: Who wrote Unix, mostly in C?
exercises.explanation: Unix was rewritten in C in 1973. That made it easy to move to other computers, and it spread everywhere.
